nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the detective novel of character and the theological drama
literary_identity: Novelist, translator and dramatist; the finest stylist of the Golden Age detective novel, the creator of Lord Peter Wimsey and Harriet Vane, and the translator of Dante.
biography: Born Dorothy Leigh Sayers in Oxford on 13 June 1893, the daughter of a clergyman and schoolmaster; she took a first in medieval literature at Somerville and worked in publishing and advertising. Whose Body? (1923) introduced Lord Peter Wimsey; Strong Poison (1930), The Nine Tailors (1934) and Gaudy Night (1935) are the finest English detective novels of the period. She gave up fiction in the late 1930s for theological drama (The Man Born to Be King, 1941) and her Penguin translation of Dante's Inferno (1949). She died at Witham, Essex, on 17 December 1957.
literary_profile: Sayers is the finest writer of the Golden Age detective novel: The Nine Tailors is the most perfectly constructed English mystery, Gaudy Night is the first detective novel built on the inner life of a woman intellectual, and her Lord Peter Wimsey — with Harriet Vane — is the most fully realised detective in English fiction. Her theological plays made Christian drama a popular form, and her Dante translation is still the standard Penguin edition.
stylistic_characteristics: The fair-play plot carried by character rather than mechanism; the detective novel as a novel of manners; the donnish wit and the literary allusion; the English village, the bell-ringing and the ecclesiastical setting; the love plot developed across several volumes.
intellectual_concerns: Murder and the closed community; the English village, the church and the bell tower; money, marriage and the family; the woman intellectual and the price of her education; guilt, forgiveness and Christian doctrine; the detection as a search for truth.
historical_significance: Sayers is the finest stylist of the Golden Age and the period's most accomplished woman of letters: The Nine Tailors and Gaudy Night are the finest detective novels in English, her theological drama made Christian broadcasting a popular form, and her Dante is the standard modern English translation. She gave the genre its first fully realised woman intellectual.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the antiquarian ghost story and the scholarly supernatural tale
literary_identity: Medievalist, palaeographer and ghost-story writer; the greatest English writer of ghost stories and the Provost of Eton.
biography: Born Montague Rhodes James at Goodnestone, Kent, on 1 August 1862; he was educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, where he spent his working life as a scholar of medieval manuscripts and became Provost of King's (1905) and then of Eton (1918). Ghost Stories of an Antiquary appeared in 1904, More Ghost Stories in 1911, A Thin Ghost in 1919 and A Warning to the Curious in 1925; his catalogue of the Cambridge manuscripts is a foundation of medieval scholarship. He died at Eton on 12 June 1936.
literary_profile: James invented the modern English ghost story: his four collections gave the genre its antiquarian form — the scholar, the document, the exact topography, the withheld apparition — and his stories ('Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad', 'Casting the Runes', 'A Warning to the Curious') are the finest in the language. He is also one of the great medieval scholars of the century, and the combination of the two is what makes his stories work.
stylistic_characteristics: The antiquarian frame: the discovery of a document, an object or a manuscript; the dry, exact scholarly tone; the English landscape and the English county named precisely; the withheld apparition and the deliberately unexplained ending; the short story delivered on Christmas Eve.
intellectual_concerns: The unquiet dead and the violated grave; antiquity and the recovered object; the scholar's curiosity and its punishment; the English landscape as a place of buried history; the limits of knowledge; the horror of the ordinary and the domestic.
historical_significance: James is the greatest English writer of ghost stories and the founder of the modern supernatural tale: his four collections established the antiquarian form, 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and 'Casting the Runes' are the finest stories of their kind, and his scholarly authority gave the genre a seriousness it had lacked. He is the central figure of the movement recorded here.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the supernatural tale of nature and the ghost story of the open air
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest English writer of supernatural nature fiction and one of the masters of the Edwardian ghost story.
biography: Born Algernon Henry Blackwood at Shooter's Hill, Kent, on 14 March 1869; he worked in Canada as a hotel manager, a journalist and a farmer, returned to England in 1899, and joined the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. The Empty House (1906), John Silence (1908), The Centaur (1911) and Incredible Adventures (1914) made him famous; he broadcast regularly on the BBC, wrote some thirty books, and died at Bishopsteignton, Devon, on 10 December 1951.
literary_profile: Blackwood is the great English writer of supernatural nature fiction: 'The Willows' and 'The Wendigo' are among the finest stories of the supernatural ever written, and their terror comes not from the ghost but from the landscape itself. He is the missing link between the Victorian ghost story and the modern weird tale, and Lovecraft named him a master.
stylistic_characteristics: The landscape as protagonist; the slow accumulation of dread without an apparition; the traveller and the camping expedition; the prose that renders the natural world as sentient; the unexplained ending; the first-person narrative of the sensitive observer.
intellectual_concerns: Nature as a living and hostile power; the wilderness, the river and the forest; the primitive and the ancient; the limits of human knowledge; the spiritualist and the occult; the solitary traveller and the loss of self.
historical_significance: Blackwood wrote the finest supernatural nature fiction in English: 'The Willows' and 'The Wendigo' are permanent tales, his landscape-based terror gave the ghost story a new subject, and his influence runs through Lovecraft and the modern weird tale. He is the period's great writer of the outdoors supernatural.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Welsh; the tale of the pagan survival and the horror of the ancient world
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and journalist; the great Welsh writer of supernatural horror and the author of 'The Great God Pan' and The Hill of Dreams.
biography: Born Arthur Llewellyn Jones at Caerleon, Monmouthshire, on 3 March 1863; he failed to get into medicine, worked as a clerk, a tutor and a journalist, and published The Great God Pan and The Inmost Light in 1894 and The Three Impostors in 1895. The Hill of Dreams followed in 1907, The Bowmen — the story that created the Angel of Mons — in 1915, and a stream of essays, translations and memoirs thereafter. He died at Beaconsfield on 15 December 1947.
literary_profile: Machen is the great Welsh writer of supernatural horror: The Great God Pan is the most influential English horror story of the 1890s, The Hill of Dreams is one of the finest decadent novels in the language, and 'The White People' is the strangest story of its kind in English. His paganism and his Welsh landscape gave the ghost story a mythology, and Lovecraft and Stephen King both acknowledge him.
stylistic_characteristics: The tale built on an ancient survival beneath the modern town; the Welsh landscape and the Roman ruins; the decadent novel of the artist's vision; the document and the hearsay that never quite resolve; the prose of ecstatic description; the horror that is never shown.
intellectual_concerns: The pagan survival and the ancient world beneath the modern; Wales, the Roman past and the Celtic inheritance; the artist's vision and its cost; the city (London) as a place of corruption; the body and the sexual secret; the occult and the esoteric.
historical_significance: Machen wrote the most influential English horror story of the 1890s and one of the finest decadent novels: The Great God Pan shaped the whole modern genre, The Hill of Dreams is a permanent novel of the artist, and 'The White People' is the strangest story in English. He gave the supernatural tale a mythology and a Welsh landscape.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comedy of manners, the revue and the popular song
literary_identity: Playwright, composer, actor and director; the most performed English dramatist of the period and the definitive voice of interwar sophistication.
biography: Born Noël Pierce Coward at Teddington on 16 December 1899; he went on the stage as a child, wrote his first play at eleven and served in the army in the First World War. The Young Idea (1923), The Vortex (1924), Hay Fever (1925), Bitter Sweet (1929), Private Lives (1930), Cavalcade (1931), Design for Living (1933), Blithe Spirit (1941) and Brief Encounter (1945) made him the most successful playwright of his time; he wrote the songs, composed the music and directed and starred in the productions. He was knighted in 1970 and died in Jamaica on 26 March 1973.
literary_profile: Coward is the most performed English dramatist of the period and the definitive voice of interwar sophistication: Private Lives and Hay Fever are the finest English comedies of manners of the century, Blithe Spirit is the best English comedy of the supernatural, and Brief Encounter (from his one-act Still Life) is one of the great English films. His songs — 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen', 'Mad About the Boy', 'Someday I'll Find You' — are the period's lyric poetry of the drawing room.
stylistic_characteristics: The epigram and the witty exchange; the symmetrical three-act construction; the single drawing-room set; the sophisticated, amoral, unillusioned tone; the song written into the action; the revue's sketch structure and the musical's integration of song and scene.
intellectual_concerns: Love, marriage and infidelity among the leisured; the country house weekend and the Riviera hotel; the pursuit of pleasure and the fear of boredom; the changing position of women; class, money and the nouveaux riches; the English abroad.
historical_significance: Coward is the most performed English dramatist of the period: Private Lives and Hay Fever are the finest comedies of manners of the century, Blithe Spirit and Brief Encounter are permanent, and his songs and revues made him the voice of interwar England. He is the period's definitive comic dramatist.
